b: Insights · Data & BI “We can't do AI until the data's sorted” The foundations project has a start date, a budget and a steering committee. What it doesn't have is a finish date. Guide It's reasonable advice — the master data's a mess, the ERP doesn't talk to the planning tool, three systems hold a version of the customer that none of them agree on. But the foundations project has a start date, a budget and a steering committee. What it doesn't have, and never has, is a finish date. 66% Efficiency gain of finance teams using AI report greater efficiency and productivity 63% Slower than expected said implementation went slower than expected in 2025 Gartner, March 2026 survey of 204 finance leaders Where the blocker actually moves to You can export a file today, point a model at it with the right instructions and proper checks, and it will do work that used to take a week — no integration project required. But a few weeks in, the constraint stops being the data and becomes the person reading the output. Who on the team can look at a plausible, beautifully formatted answer and spot the assumption that's quietly wrong? Who's curious enough to keep taking the process apart rather than accepting the first draft? That's the real audit — and it can't happen while everyone is still waiting for the systems project to land. What this means in practice 01 Pick one process this month Choose something that doesn't need a system change to try — board commentary, a reconciliation, a first-draft forecast. Export, upload, run it properly, then compare the result to what a person produced. One process, four weeks, a real answer either way. 02 Write the checks before the prompt Traceable formulas and a documented source for every assumption, before you write a word to the model. A marketing team can live with an odd hallucination in a first draft; someone will ask you where a number came from eleven months after you produced it, and the answer needs to exist. 03 Keep the systems roadmap running Same pace, same budget, no pause. This is what you do while the foundations are being laid, not instead of doing it — the teams that get this wrong pick one and quietly drop the other. 04 Watch who takes to it The person who rebuilds the output twice because the first version wasn't good enough has just told you something a competency framework never would. They're your next AI-in-Finance champion — and possibly the case for keeping someone else exactly where they are. The data will never be finished — that's just what data looks like in a growing business, with another acquisition, another product line, another system somebody bought without asking. The better question is whether you're willing to work in the house while it's being fixed, and whether the people in there with you are the ones you'd want alongside you when it's done. The systems project will take eighteen months. One exported file can start on Tuesday. b: Insights · Reporting & governance · Exit & M&A Board reporting a buyer will trust Diligence doesn't begin at the data room. It begins with twenty-four months of board packs. Guide The pack, the challenge, the gaps 01 The monthly pack One summary page first. Revenue, gross margin, EBITDA, cash, net debt and order book — actual, budget and prior year. P&L, balance sheet and cash flow together. A P&L alone says nothing about working capital. Ten working days, every month. Timeliness is itself evidence of control. Written commentary, owned by a named person. Variances explained — not a spreadsheet dump. A KPI page. The six operational numbers that drive the financial ones. Why it matters A buyer reads two years of packs in sequence. Consistency of format is being tested as hard as the content. 02 The numbers that get challenged Gross margin by customer, product and site — not one blended percentage. Normalised EBITDA and every add-back, with the evidence sitting beside it. Stock and WIP. Valuation method, provision policy, ageing profile. Revenue recognition and cut-off, particularly on contract and project work. Accruals, deferred income and rebates — anything resting on a judgement. Cash conversion. EBITDA to cash, explained rather than assumed. Why it matters Diligence tests whether your numbers behave the same way when somebody else cuts them. 03 Where the gaps usually are Management accounts that don’t bridge to the filed accounts, with no reconciliation on file. A balance sheet reviewed annually, reconciliations left to the auditor to find. No budget — or one abandoned by month four. A forecast that is a re-typed budget, rather than a rolling view of what will actually happen. Numbers that change after issue with no record of why or by whom. KPIs that measure activity, not money. Why it matters Every one of these is fixable in a quarter. None of them are fixable once diligence has started. AI and judgement — getting the balance right What the tools do well Use them, and use them properly Reconciliation, coding and matching at volume, without fatigue or drift Anomaly detection across the ledger — duplicates, outliers, missing postings Drafting first-pass variance commentary straight from the data Consolidation, data preparation and building the pack itself Answering “what is inside this number” in seconds rather than days What still needs a qualified finance mind This is what a buyer is buying Deciding what is material and what is noise Judgement calls — provisions, valuation, recognition, add-backs Knowing which variance the board actually needs to act on Owning the number in front of a buyer, an auditor or a lender The “should we actually do this deal” call Automate the preparation. Never automate the judgement. A buyer will ask who signed the number — and “the model” is not an answer. If the pack doesn’t convince your board, it will not convince a buyer. b: Insights · Reporting & governance · Leadership & culture Your boardroom doesn't need an accountant. It needs a finance leader. Being qualified to account for a business and qualified to help lead one are not the same thing. Guide There is a difference — a bloody big one. Qualifications matter, but we've spent far too long confusing being qualified to account for a business with being qualified to help lead one. Immaculate management accounts and a balance sheet reconciled to the penny are admirable. They're not the same thing as driving the business forward. The accountant Behind the Finance door Arrives at 8:30, disappears behind the Finance door. Immaculate management accounts, reconciled to the penny. Sales call them “the guy from Accounts”. Marketing aren’t entirely convinced they’ve actually met. Nobody outside Finance knows their name. The finance leader In the business, not beside it Everywhere — talking to Sales, understanding Operations, annoying Marketing. Speaks to customers, asks questions, actually understands how the business works. People tell them things before decisions are made. Involved before the expensive call, not explaining it afterwards. Commercial instinct, relationships and influence, not just controls. The numbers tell you what Margin fell. Aged debt is rising. Headcount is up. The P&L, the debtor ledger and the payroll report each state a fact — reliably, and after it's already happened. People tell you why Credit Control knows why customers aren't paying. Operations knows why one team is drowning while another has time to spare. The spreadsheet doesn't gossip — people do, and only to leaders they know and trust. Why this matters at the board table People tell things to finance leaders they know and trust. That's how Finance gets involved before an expensive decision is made — not afterwards, explaining why it was expensive. So yes, give me brilliant accountants — technical expertise, controls, compliance and accurate reporting. But at the boardroom table, give me someone with commercial instinct, curiosity, operational understanding, relationships and influence too — someone who understands the numbers and the business that creates them. Those things don't come printed on a certificate. Being qualified to account for a business and qualified to lead one are not the same thing. The distinction Finance provides the what and the why. Facilitation unlocks the how. That is often the difference between a good CFO and an exceptional one. In a world that demands better problem-solving, perhaps the true value of a CFO isn't just in controlling performance — but in enabling it. Process is necessary and insufficient — not optional. Briefing Briefing note · September 2026 It is an odd thing for a finance director to argue that process is not the differentiator. Process is most of what finance people are hired to build: controls, reporting cycles, forecasting discipline, approval limits, month-end. Get those wrong and nothing else you do will save the business. But process is the floor, not the ceiling. It is also, in almost every case, copyable. A competitor can buy the same ERP, engage the same advisers, adopt the same framework and hire people out of the same firms. Within a year or two they can have a control environment indistinguishable from yours. What they cannot copy is how people in your business behave when nobody is checking. Whether a twenty-four-year-old will challenge a fifty-eight-year-old in a meeting, and whether the fifty-eight-year-old will change their mind. Whether bad news travels upward quickly or slowly. Whether the best idea wins or the most senior one does. The argument in short Process is what stops a business failing. Culture is what makes it win. Confusing the two, in either direction, is expensive. And the honest version of the claim: mixing ages does not improve performance by itself. It improves performance only where the culture converts the difference into something useful. That is precisely the point. 1 · Culture is a measurable financial variable 23% Higher profitability top-quartile engagement versus bottom quartile 78% Lower absenteeism the swing that lands directly in EBITDA 70% Down to the manager share of the variance in team engagement Gallup Q12 meta-analysis: 183,806 business units, 53 industries, 90 countries. Turnover is 21% lower, or 51% lower in low-turnover organisations, and wellbeing 70% higher. The long-run study, and its caveats Kotter and Heskett examined more than 200 companies across 22 industries over eleven years to 1990. Firms whose cultures emphasised all key constituencies — customers, shareholders and employees — and encouraged leadership at every level outperformed the rest by a wide margin: revenue growth averaging 682% against 166%, share price growth 901% against 74%, net income growth 756% against 1%. Two caveats rarely travel with those figures. The data ends in 1990, so it describes a different economy. And a study of this design cannot fully separate cause from effect — successful firms can afford better cultures, as well as the reverse. Directionally powerful rather than conclusive. Where culture actually comes from Culture is not created by a values statement or an away-day. It is created, or destroyed, by what individual managers do on ordinary Tuesdays. For context on the size of the prize: Gallup puts global engagement at around 20–23%, with the cost of disengagement estimated at $8.8–10 trillion in lost productivity — roughly 9% of global GDP. Most organisations are competing against a very low bar. 2 · The founder-age myth The dominant story about high-growth business is a young one: the university dropout, the garage, the twenty-three-year-old chief executive. It is a story that shapes who gets funded, who gets promoted and who quietly concludes they are too old to start something. It is also, on the evidence, wrong. Mean founder age by growth band All new firms 41.9 Top 1% growth 43.7 Top 0.1% growth 45.0 Successful exit 46.7 Azoulay, Jones, Kim & Miranda, ‘Age and High-Growth Entrepreneurship’, American Economic Review: Insights — US Census Bureau and IRS records for 2.7 million people who founded businesses between 2007 and 2014 and went on to employ at least one person. By sector the mean was 43.2 in high technology, 42 among venture-backed firms and 45 among patent-holding firms. The authors estimate a 50-year-old founder is roughly 1.8 times as likely as a 30-year-old to create a top 0.1% growth firm — approximately twice as likely. They found no evidence that founders in their twenties are especially likely to succeed. The mechanism they identify is not age itself but accumulated, specific knowledge: prior experience in the same industry predicts substantially higher rates of success. What looks like an advantage of age is really an advantage of having seen the problem before. The garage prodigy is not imaginary. But once you look past a small gallery of famous technology companies to millions of real founders, exceptional growth correlates with middle age, not youth. 3 · Where the young founder story is right None of which makes youth a liability. The pattern in the strongest young-founder businesses is consistent: the founder brought something the experienced operator could not, and then deliberately went and found the experience they lacked. The instinct that built the brand — giving free product to fitness YouTubers at an expo, building a community rather than buying advertising — is not an instinct a fifty-five-year-old retail executive would have had. The more instructive part came next. With revenue around £4.5m and the business straining under its own growth, he brought in Paul Richardson — born 1959, a serial entrepreneur who had built and sold a waste business and helped rescue AllSaints — as executive chairman, and Steve Hewitt as CEO. He stepped down at twenty-three, following honest 360-degree feedback from his own leadership team. Within roughly three years sales passed £100m and pre-tax profits reached £18m. Guide The sequence — and the order matters 01 Governance first A board that actually meets. A date, a pack, a decision, minutes. The kitchen table is not governance. Separate the three tables. Family, board and management — same people, different hats, different meetings. A family charter. How decisions get made, how disputes get settled, how a family member joins the business. One voice from outside the family. Someone at the table with no inheritance at stake. Dividend policy written down before the year it becomes contentious. Why it matters Governance is the only one of the three you can build while everyone still agrees. It is what carries the family through the point where they don’t. 02 Roles second Real jobs with real accountabilities — applied to family and non-family alike. Market rate for the role performed, not for the surname. An honest answer on whether they want it. Asked properly, asked privately, and believed. Experience earned outside before a senior seat inside. A route for capable non-family managers — or you lose them at precisely the wrong moment. The founder’s role defined by a date, not by feel. Why it matters Most succession failures are not about who owns the shares. They are about someone holding a job they could not do, or never wanted. 03 Ownership third A structure that separates economic value from control where those two things need to sit apart. A shareholders’ agreement. Pre-emption, valuation method, deadlock, and a way out for a family member who wants one. Wills, trusts and reliefs reviewed together, not by three advisers separately — and kept current as the rules move. A valuation everyone has seen, on a method everyone has agreed, before anyone needs it. Fairness for those not in the business — settled deliberately, not left to a will. Test it against a death, a divorce and a falling-out, not just a retirement. Why it matters Ownership decisions are slow to reverse and expensive to get wrong. Take them once governance and roles are settled, and they get far easier. Staying involved after the handover Where it works Defined, visible, time-bound A defined role with a defined end date, in writing, seen by the management team Chairman or non-executive — contributing at the board, not shadowing the MD Customer, supplier and technical relationships handed over deliberately, one by one Any earn-out tied to things the seat you hold can still influence A successor you back in public, including when you disagree in private Where it goes wrong The failure modes we see most “I’ll stay involved” — with no shared definition of involved Staff who keep walking past the new MD’s office to reach yours An earn-out resting on decisions somebody else now makes A retained minority stake with no mechanism to realise it No answer to what you do on the Monday after The question is not whether you stay involved. It is whether everyone can describe what involved means — in one sentence, and the same sentence. Governance, then roles, then ownership. Any other order costs more. b: Insights · IFRS & standards · Reporting & governance IFRS 18 is coming: what growing businesses need to know (and do now) The biggest change to how companies present their performance in over 20 years. Profit doesn't change — how you show it, explain it and back it up does. LinkedIn article · 1 Nov 2026 If your business reports under IFRS, your income statement is about to look different. IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements replaces IAS 1 for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027, and is widely described as the biggest change to how companies present their performance in more than 20 years. The reassuring part first: IFRS 18 does not change how much profit you make. Recognition and measurement stay the same, and the balance sheet barely moves. What changes is how your results are structured, labelled and explained, and the data your finance team needs to produce them. The less reassuring part: the standard applies retrospectively, so a December year-end business will need to restate its 2026 comparatives. In other words, the work starts a full year before the first IFRS 18 year end, not at it. First things first: does IFRS 18 apply to you? If your company prepares its accounts under FRS 102, IFRS 18 does not apply to your statutory accounts. That covers most UK SMEs, so it is worth saying plainly before anything else. But plenty of growing businesses are pulled into the IFRS world in other ways. IFRS 18 is likely to matter to you if: You report under UK-adopted IFRS. That includes AIM-quoted groups and private companies that have chosen IFRS. The UK Endorsement Board endorsed IFRS 18 for UK use on 10 December 2025. You are a subsidiary of a group that reports under IFRS. Even if your own accounts are FRS 102, your parent will need your group reporting pack in the new IFRS 18 shape. You use FRS 101, the reduced disclosure framework. FRS 101 is built on IFRS, so the new income statement structure reaches you. The FRC has granted some relief: FRS 101 reporters are exempt from the new performance-measure disclosures and from part of the new expense-by-nature analysis. You are heading for a sale, new investor or refinancing. An IFRS-reporting acquirer, private equity house or lender will look at your numbers through the IFRS 18 lens, whatever framework you use today. Not sure which box you sit in? That is a ten-minute conversation, and a good place to start. The six changes that matter most IFRS 18 runs to well over a hundred paragraphs, but for an owner-managed or mid-sized business these six do the heavy lifting. 01 A new shape for the income statement Every line of income and expense must sit in one of five categories: operating, investing, financing, income taxes or discontinued operations. Operating is the default home for anything that does not belong elsewhere. 02 Two new required subtotals You must show operating profit and profit before financing and income taxes . For the first time, “operating profit” has a fixed definition, so your new figure may not match the one you report today. 03 Your adjusted profit figures come under the spotlight If you quote measures such as adjusted EBITDA or underlying operating profit in public communications, IFRS 18 calls these management-defined performance measures. They must be explained in a single note in the audited accounts: why you use them, how you calculate them, and a reconciliation to the nearest IFRS subtotal, showing the tax and minority-interest effect of each adjustment. 04 No more hiding in “other” New grouping principles mean material items must be broken out, and “other” may only be used when no more informative label exists. Large sundry lines will be challenged. 05 More detail behind your cost lines If you present expenses by function (cost of sales, distribution, admin), you must disclose how much depreciation, amortisation, employee benefits, impairment losses and inventory write-downs sit within each line. Many ledgers do not capture that today. 06 A tidier, but different, cash flow statement Under the indirect method, the starting point becomes operating profit. For most trading businesses, interest paid must now be shown in financing and interest and dividends received in investing, with the old policy choices removed. Your reported operating cash flow may change even though your bank balance does not. The balance sheet sees only minor changes. Why the work starts early IFRS 18 applies retrospectively. A business with a 31 December year end will publish its first IFRS 18 accounts for 2027, but the 2026 comparatives must be restated in the new format too. The standard also asks for something extra in that first year: a reconciliation, line by line, between the 2026 income statement as originally presented under IAS 1 and the restated IFRS 18 version. Groups that publish half-year reports under IAS 34 face this sooner, in their first interim report of 2027. IFRS 18: the key dates For a business with a 31 December year end Apr 2024 IASB issues IFRS 18 Dec 2025 Endorsed for UK use 1 Jan 2026 Comparative year begins 1 Jan 2027 IFRS 18 effective 30 Jun 2027 First half-year reports (interim reporters) 31 Dec 2027 First IFRS 18 year end, 2026 restated IFRS 18 applies retrospectively: 2026 figures must be restated, with a line-by-line reconciliation to the old presentation. In practice, that means the data you capture during 2026 needs to support the new categories and disclosures. Mapping it as you go is far easier than reconstructing it from an old trial balance in 2028. More than a formatting exercise It is tempting to treat IFRS 18 as a job for the year-end accounts template. The businesses that handle it well will look further, because the changes ripple into everyday finance: Chart of accounts and ledger coding. Each nominal code needs a home in the new categories, and some may need splitting to capture expenses by nature. Reporting and consolidation tools. Templates, mappings and group reporting packs will need rebuilding, and tested before the first year end. Banking covenants. Check whether your facility definitions refer to reported operating profit or operating cash flow, or are protected by a “frozen GAAP” clause. A presentation change could move a covenant calculation without anything real changing. Bonus schemes, earn-outs and share plans. Targets linked to “operating profit” may need clarifying before the definition shifts underneath them. Board packs and KPIs. Aligning management reporting with the new subtotals avoids running two versions of the truth. Your auditor. Agreeing classification judgements early avoids a difficult conversation at year end. Where an experienced hand helps Most finance teams in growing businesses are already stretched by month-end, audit and forecasting. A standards change is exactly the kind of one-off project that slips down the list until it becomes urgent. That is where Themis Professional Services can help. Run an impact assessment on your latest accounts, showing what your income statement and cash flow statement would look like under IFRS 18. Map your chart of accounts to the new categories and set up the data you need for restated comparatives. Review covenants, bonus schemes and earn-outs that rely on profit definitions. Prepare the performance-measure note and talk it through with your auditor. The aim is simple: no surprises at year end, and a finance function that comes out of the change stronger. b: Insights · Leadership & culture Kodak buried its best idea. Bumble might be next. Two companies. Same mistake, thirty years apart. Rework your strategy to avoid the same. LinkedIn post · 5 Sep 2026 Kodak invented the digital camera in 1975, then buried it, because film paid the bills. By 1996 it had two-thirds of the global photography market and $16bn in revenue. By 2012 it was bankrupt. The thing that made Kodak great — controlling how, when and how few pictures you took — was exactly what digital photography destroyed. Bumble, the online dating app, is doing something similar, in real time. Its one distinctive rule, women message first, solved a genuine problem: women drowning in messages, men getting almost none. It took the company to a $14bn IPO in 2021. But paying users and revenue are now both falling, the share price is down roughly 95% since listing, and Bumble has quietly let men message first and stretched its reply window from 24 hours to 72 — dismantling the one thing that made it different from Tinder or Hinge. Kodak 1975 – 2012 Bumble 2014 – today The distinctive thing Control of how, when and how few pictures you took. Women message first. What it was worth Two-thirds of the global photography market and $16bn revenue by 1996. A $14bn IPO in 2021. What happened to it Protected until digital photography removed it entirely. Bankrupt by 2012. Being dismantled by choice — men may now message first, and the reply window has gone from 24 hours to 72. Where that leaves them The market moved and the USP became worthless. Paying users and revenue falling, share price down roughly 95% since listing. Where the two stories meet We used to meet someone, then take a photo of the moment. Dating apps and camera phones flipped that order entirely: now you see the photo first, swipe, message — and the actual meeting comes last, if it comes at all. And the generation that grew up entirely inside that flipped order is now rejecting it on both fronts. Gen Z is driving a genuine boom in film and disposable cameras — Kodak itself just launched a new one — precisely because it's slower, scarcer and more deliberate than a camera roll. The same generation is telling researchers they're burnt out on swiping and want fewer, more intentional matches, and real dates, not more messages. Kodak protected its USP until the market removed it entirely. Bumble is dismantling its own USP just as the market seems to be asking for exactly what it originally offered. Same lesson, opposite directions Know precisely what makes you different, and keep testing — deliberately, regularly — whether the market still wants it. It changes more often than most strategies assume. b: Insights · Tax Tax planning for UK SMEs: timing, reliefs and the decisions that matter Almost every planning point here is a timing point. Very few reduce the total tax paid — most change when it is paid, and what it costs in cash along the way. Briefing Technical briefing · September 2026 Good tax planning for a UK SME is rarely about clever structuring. In practice it is about getting the timing right on decisions the business would be making anyway: when to invest in equipment, when to invest in research and development, how and when directors take money out of the company, when to declare a dividend, and when to start thinking seriously about succession. Two Budgets in the last two years, together with reforms already legislated for 2026, have moved most of the dials that owner-managed businesses rely on. Capital allowances, R&D relief, the charge on overdrawn director’s loan accounts, dividend tax rates, employee share schemes, Business Asset Disposal Relief and Business Property Relief have all changed. Several changed twice. Why the distinction matters Full expensing is a timing difference rather than a permanent saving — it accelerates relief that would otherwise arrive over several years, and it is clawed back on disposal. The value is in the cash flow and in the rate at which relief is obtained, not in the headline percentage. The same is true of loss relief, instalment payments and most extraction planning. Companies, sole traders and most partnerships; new and second-hand assets; now a permanent feature. Full expensing — uncapped. Companies only, new and unused main-pool plant and machinery. Not assets bought for leasing, not cars, not second-hand. 50% FYA on new special rate expenditure. Sequence the claims. Point AIA at expenditure that would otherwise attract only the special rate, since full expensing cannot reach it at 100%. Why it matters Run together properly, a company can get 100% on up to £1m of second-hand or special-rate spend through AIA while using uncapped full expensing for new main-pool assets. 02 Two changes that alter the calculus From 1 January 2026, a new 40% first-year allowance applies to qualifying main-rate plant and machinery not covered by AIA or full expensing. From 1 April 2026, the main pool writing-down allowance falls from 18% to 14%. Expenditure left in the general pool now takes roughly a quarter longer to write down. Straddling periods are calculated on a blended basis, apportioned by days either side of the change. Why it matters The slower the pool unwinds, the more the year in which you buy is worth arguing about. 03 The disposal trap Full expensing carries a clawback AIA does not. Disposal proceeds come in as an immediate balancing charge under CAA 2001 s59A, not as a reduction of the pool. Claimed on the whole cost? The charge equals the whole disposal value. On part, a proportion applies. On 50% FYA assets, half the disposal value. For kit you’ll sell on soon, AIA or writing-down allowances may leave the company better off. The fixed asset register becomes compliance, not housekeeping — cost, date, and which allowance was claimed. Why it matters Front-loading relief that is then clawed back in full is not a saving. It is a loan. Buildings Non-residential construction, renovation and conversion falls outside the plant and machinery regime and attracts the Structures and Buildings Allowance: 3% straight line over 33⅓ years, on contracts from 29 October 2018. No first-year relief, no acceleration — the only timing decision is when the building is brought into use. An allowance statement is a statutory requirement, and a buyer of a used structure must obtain a copy from the previous owner. b: Insights · Tax Six tax timing points UK SME owners are getting wrong in 2026 Most tax planning for an owner-managed business isn't structuring. It's sequencing — and several of the dates moved this year. LinkedIn post · 6 Sep 2026 Most tax planning for an owner-managed business isn't structuring. It's sequencing — and several of the dates moved this year. The six 01 Full expensing isn't automatically the right claim 100% relief looks obviously better than 14%. But dispose of an asset you've fully expensed and the whole disposal value returns as a balancing charge (CAA 2001 s59A) — a standalone taxable amount, not netted off the pool. For kit you'll sell on in a few years while it still holds value, AIA or writing-down allowances can leave you better off. The main pool WDA also fell from 18% to 14% on 1 April 2026. 02 ERIS isn't automatically better than the merged R&D scheme ERIS is worth up to ~27p per £1 against the merged scheme's 14.7–16.2p. But it's only for loss-making SMEs at 30%+ R&D intensity, and that 27p assumes losses to surrender. Near break-even there's little to surrender and the flat merged rate can win. Harder still: first-time claimants, or anyone who hasn't claimed in three years, must notify HMRC within six months of the period end. Miss it and the claim is gone. 03 An overdrawn director's loan carries two separate charges s455 rose to 35.75% for loans outstanding from 6 April 2026. Repaying £5k+ then redrawing within 30 days is disregarded, and the refund doesn't arrive until nine months after the end of the period in which you repaid. Separately: if the balance tops £10,000 at any point and you charge below HMRC's official rate (3.75%), that's a benefit in kind — income tax for you, Class 1A at 15% for the company. Charging interest fixes the second charge and does nothing for the first. 04 Two deductions depend on cash actually moving Accrued remuneration is only deductible in the period accrued if paid within nine months of the year end (CTA 2009 s1288) — catching holiday pay accruals, not just director bonuses. Employer pension contributions are deductible only when paid in cleared funds (FA 2004 s196). An accrual won't do. 05 Count your associated companies The £50k/£250k corporation tax thresholds, the £1.5m instalment threshold and the £5m loss deductions allowance are all divided by associated companies plus one. The marginal rate between £50k and £250k is 26.5% — above the 25% headline — so deductible spend is worth more inside the band than above it. 06 Exit and succession got more expensive — but less than widely reported BADR is 18% from 6 April 2026 on a £1m lifetime limit. BPR is now capped — but at £2.5m of combined business and agricultural property, not the £1m still being quoted. That was the original 2024 proposal, raised in December 2025 and now law. It's transferable between spouses, so £5m for a couple, with 50% relief above. The point None of this is exotic. b: Insights · Leadership & culture Unfair dismissal from 1 January 2027 The qualifying period falls to six months and the cap on compensation is abolished. A bounded liability with a known ceiling becomes an open-ended one — at the point when the queue to find out has never been longer. Briefing Technical briefing · September 2026 On 1 January 2027 the qualifying period for ordinary unfair dismissal falls from two years to six months, and the cap on the compensatory award is abolished altogether. Both changes come from the Employment Rights Act 2025, which received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025 and is being commenced in stages across 2026 and 2027. Most commentary treats this as a human resources problem. It is also a financial one. A contested dismissal ceases to be a bounded liability with a known ceiling and becomes an open-ended contingent liability that, given current tribunal waiting times, may remain unresolved for two to four years. That is a provisioning question and a due diligence question as much as an employment question. The change in one line It is not that dismissal becomes harder. It is that the consequence of getting it wrong stops having a ceiling, at exactly the point when the queue to find out has never been longer. The changes apply in England, Scotland and Wales. Unfair dismissal is devolved in Northern Ireland, where a separate package of reform is planned. 1 · What changes on 1 January 2027 Measure Now From 1 January 2027 Qualifying period, ‘ordinary’ unfair dismissal 2 years 6 months Right to request written reasons for dismissal 2 years 6 months Unfair dismissal for reason of spent convictions 2-year qualifying period No qualifying period Cap on the compensatory award Lower of £123,543 or 52 weeks’ gross pay No cap Basis of calculating the award Actual and projected loss, evidenced by the claimant Unchanged Day-one protections (discrimination, automatically unfair dismissal) Apply from day one Unchanged Employment Rights Act 2025, s25 and Schedule 3; Department for Business and Trade unfair dismissal factsheet. The cap figure is that applying from 6 April 2026. Section 25 reduces the qualifying period to six months and also removes the power to vary that period by secondary legislation — any future change requires primary legislation, which gives employers more planning certainty than the position that has applied since the period moved to two years in April 2012. Schedule 3 makes the corresponding reduction for written reasons and removes the qualifying period entirely for spent-conviction dismissals. Section 124 of the Employment Rights Act 1996, which contains the cap, is repealed in full. The government has confirmed it does not intend to consult further, and the dates should be treated as firm. 2 · Commencement mechanics — who is actually caught 01 There is no phase-in From 1 January 2027, any employee who already has six months’ service is protected immediately. No transitional ramp, no grandfathering of existing staff. In practical terms, anyone engaged from 1 July 2026 onwards who is still employed on 1 January 2027 will have the necessary service. Everyone hired before that date is covered from day one of the new regime. 02 Statutory notice counts as service, whether or not you give it The effective date of termination is extended by the statutory minimum notice period, regardless of whether that notice was given or worked. Between one month and two years’ service, the statutory minimum is one week. So an employee dismissed in late December 2026 without working notice may have their termination date pushed into January 2027, and qualify under the six-month rule rather than the two-year rule. Broadly, around twenty-five weeks of actual service will be enough. Act on this Any dismissal planned for December 2026 needs this checked before notice is given. 03 The two changes commence differently They are usually described as one package, but they do not bite on identical populations. The uncapped regime applies only where the actual date of termination falls on or after 1 January 2027. An employee cannot rely on an extended effective date to reach it, even though an extended date can carry them into the six-month qualifying period. A December 2026 dismissal could therefore give rise to a claim that would not otherwise have existed — but that claim would still be subject to the cap. The distinction is narrow and worth confirming with an adviser in any specific case. 3 · What does not change Day-one protection against discrimination is unaffected, as is day-one protection against automatically unfair dismissal — whistleblowing, trade union activity, health and safety, asserting a statutory right, and the rest. The basis of compensation is unchanged. Awards remain based on actual and projected loss, evidenced by the claimant, subject to what the tribunal considers just and equitable. Removing the cap does not create a new head of loss; it removes a ceiling. Notice periods are unchanged, both statutory and contractual. Non-renewal of a fixed-term contract on expiry remains a dismissal. Where the employee has six months’ service, non-renewal will need to be a fair dismissal — materially affecting businesses running seasonal or project-based arrangements. Protection still applies only to employees, not to workers or the genuinely self-employed. Wider employment status reform is under discussion but nothing is legislated. 4 · How this affects an employer’s current position Probation periods no longer function as a buffer A live change, not a theoretical one A six-month probation period — the most common length in UK practice — will now expire at almost exactly the moment protection begins. Allowing for the statutory notice extension, protection may in fact arrive slightly before probation ends. A probation framework designed on the old assumptions is now actively working against the employer. Legal commentary has converged on three to four months, with a clearly drafted and sparingly used right to extend by around a month, to force the assessment decision to a point where there is still room to act. Around 40% of businesses operate a discretionary probationary period, and the substantial majority are six months or shorter. Performance management has to become earlier and evidenced Not a new standard — a much larger group A concern identified at month four or five could previously be handled with some informality. Now, delay risks the employee acquiring protection before any decision is reached. The requirement is documented objectives from the start, recorded review conversations at defined points, and a decision taken deliberately rather than by drift. This is the same fair-process standard that has always applied at two years’ service. Businesses that already manage performance properly face little additional exposure; those that have relied on the qualifying period as a substitute for management face a great deal. The financial exposure changes shape, not just size 646 Reported awards unfair dismissal awards in employment tribunals, 2023/24 £6,746 Median award for the overwhelming majority of claims the cap was never the operative constraint No cap Where losses are large senior managers, long notice periods, bonus or share-based earnings, long periods out of the market Removing the cap matters far less than the headlines suggest for typical cases, and far more for a specific group. It becomes the operative constraint precisely where a finance director should be looking: the senior population where a single claim can become material. A secondary effect is on settlement dynamics. Where a cap exists, both sides negotiate against a known worst case. Removing it widens the range of credible outcomes and, at the margin, increases the price of settling — particularly for higher earners. This is a balance sheet question, not only an HR one Employment litigation that used to be a note in due diligence becomes a number. Given tribunal waiting times, a contested dismissal of a senior employee now represents an uncapped contingent liability that may sit unresolved across two or three reporting periods — with consequences for provisioning, audit discussion, disclosure, and warranty and disclosure schedules on any transaction. 5 · Why this is good for employees 6.3 million people 22% of everyone employed aged 16 and over have been with their current employer for between six months and two years. Under current law that group has only very limited protection: they can be dismissed without a fair reason and without a fair process, with no recourse unless the dismissal is discriminatory or automatically unfair. From January 2027 they gain the right to a fair reason and a fair process, the right to written reasons, and access to a tribunal if neither is provided.
